desc:
A class of n students labelled 0 to n - 1 must be split into two teams. Every student joins exactly one team, and a team may be empty. The list dislikes contains pairs [a, b] meaning that students a and b cannot be on the same team.

Among all valid splits, find the smallest possible difference between the sizes of the two teams, that is the minimum of |size(team 1) - size(team 2)|. If no valid split exists, return -1.

n = 5, dislikes = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,4]]  ->  1
(for example the teams {0,2,3} and {1,4})

n = 3, dislikes = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0]]  ->  -1
n = 4, dislikes = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]]  ->  2
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
hints: First decide whether any valid split exists at all. Which graph property is that?

Inside a connected group of students who (indirectly) dislike each other, the split is forced up to swapping the teams. So each group contributes either (x to team 1, y to team 2) or (y to team 1, x to team 2).

Compute x and y for every group by two-colouring. Then it is a subset-sum problem: which sizes of team 1 can you reach by choosing, for each group, x or y? A bitset (an integer whose bit s says 'team 1 can have size s') makes this fast: S = (S << x) | (S << y).
editorial: If the dislike graph has an odd cycle, no valid split exists and the answer is -1. Otherwise every connected component is bipartite, and its two-colouring is unique up to swapping the colours. So a component with colour classes of sizes x and y adds either x students to team 1 and y to team 2, or the other way round. Isolated students are components with sizes (1, 0).

The question becomes: choose for each component whether x or y goes to team 1, so that team 1 gets s students in total and the gap |n - 2s| is as small as possible. Keep the set of reachable values of s as a bitset stored in a Python integer: start with S = 1 (size 0) and for every component do S = (S << x) | (S << y). At the end, scan s from 0 to n and take the best |n - 2s| over the set bits.
Colouring costs O(n + m). The bitset has at most n + 1 bits, so each of at most n components costs O(n / 64) word operations. In total this is O(n + m + n<sup>2</sup>/64), tiny for n = 3,000.
